props.title: Jack Frost
props.initialSlug: A dad returns as a snowman to bond with his son

sections.content: Jack Frost stands as a peculiar entry in the family holiday genre, blending supernatural elements with grief narrative in ways that echo similar 90s films like Ghost Dad (1990) and Heart and Souls (1993). The story of a deceased father returning as a snowman manages to be both absurd and emotionally resonant, with Michael Keaton's voice work grounding the fantastical premise. The film arrived during a wave of effects-heavy family films that included Casper (1995) and Flubber (1997), showcasing the period's emerging CGI capabilities while maintaining practical effects.

sections.content: The film's treatment of loss and redemption follows a pattern established by earlier supernatural parent films like Field of Dreams (1989) and later echoed in works like The Lake House (2006). While the snowman premise might seem gimmicky, it serves as an effective metaphor for the temporary nature of parent-child relationships, particularly resonant in Jack Frost's (1998) winter setting. The knowledge that the snowman must eventually melt adds underlying tension to every scene.

Director Troy Miller brings music industry experience to the film, evident in the integration of Keaton's character's blues musician background. This musical element connects to other family films of the era like Mr. Holland's Opus (1995) and Music of the Heart (1999), where artistic passion serves as a bridge between parent and child. sections.content: Jack Frost represents a specific moment in holiday cinema when filmmakers were pushing beyond traditional Santa Claus narratives. While films like Miracle on 34th Street (1947) and The Santa Clause (1994) focused on proving Santa's existence, Jack Frost used winter imagery for more personal family stories. This trend continued with films like The Polar Express (2004) and Rise of the Guardians (2012), which expanded holiday mythology beyond conventional boundaries.
